You do not need a $20/month subscription to code with AI.

Between free tiers from major vendors and a thriving open-source ecosystem, there are real options for developers who want AI assistance without a recurring bill. The catch is understanding what "free" actually means — because every tool has trade-offs in usage limits, quality, or hidden API costs.

This guide covers the **7 best free AI coding tools in 2026**, what you actually get for $0, and where the hidden costs live.

| Tool | Type | Free Limits | Best For | Open Source |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **GitHub Copilot** | IDE extension | 2K completions/mo | Inline completions | No |
| **Cursor** | IDE | 50 premium req/mo | Visual multi-file editing | No |
| **OpenCode** | Terminal CLI | Unlimited (pay LLM) | Terminal power users | Yes |
| **Aider** | Terminal CLI | Unlimited (pay LLM) | Git-heavy refactoring | Yes |
| **Continue** | IDE extension | Unlimited (pay LLM) | IDE + open-source flexibility | Yes |
| **Gemini Code Assist** | IDE extension | Free tier | Google Cloud developers | No |
| **Amazon Q Developer** | IDE extension | Free tier | AWS infrastructure code | No |

**Bottom line:** Proprietary tools give you limited free usage. Open-source tools give you unlimited usage but shift the cost to LLM API calls. Neither path is truly $0 for serious development — but you can get remarkably close.

* * *

## 1\. GitHub Copilot Free

**Best for:** Beginners and light-use developers who want zero-friction AI completions.

GitHub Copilot remains the most widely used AI coding assistant, and its free tier is the simplest on-ramp for developers who have never tried AI coding.

### What You Get for Free

- **2,000 code completions per month** — inline suggestions as you type
- **50 chat messages per month** — ask questions about your code in the sidebar
- **Works in VS Code, JetBrains, and Neovim** — no proprietary IDE required
- **Powered by GPT and Claude models** — GitHub rotates between them

### Limitations

The free tier is enough for weekend projects and learning, but not for daily professional use. At roughly 65 completions per day, a busy developer burns through the monthly limit in a week. There is no agent mode, no multi-file editing, and no autonomous workflows on the free plan.

### Verdict

Start here if you have never used an AI coding tool. The free tier teaches you the workflow. When you hit the cap consistently, you have outgrown it.

* * *

## 2\. Cursor Free Tier

**Best for:** Visual IDE users who want to try AI-powered multi-file editing before committing to $20/month.

Cursor is the most popular AI-native IDE with over 1 million users. Its free tier gives you a taste of its flagship features — Composer for multi-file edits and tab completions — but with tight limits.

### What You Get for Free

- **50 premium model requests per month** — these power Composer and chat with top-tier models
- **500 free model requests** — unlimited use of smaller, less capable models
- **Limited tab completions** — inline suggestions with a usage cap
- **Full VS Code-based IDE experience** — import your extensions, themes, and keybindings

### Limitations

50 premium requests is roughly one productive afternoon of AI-assisted coding. Heavy Composer sessions burn through the limit fast because complex multi-file edits consume multiple requests. The free-tier models for the 500 requests are noticeably weaker on complex tasks.

### Verdict

Good for evaluation. If you spend a week in Cursor's free tier and find yourself constantly hitting limits, that is your signal to either pay $20/month or switch to an open-source tool.

* * *

## 3\. OpenCode (Open Source)

**Best for:** Terminal-native developers who want unlimited AI coding without vendor lock-in.

OpenCode is the standout open-source AI coding tool of 2026, with **95,000+ GitHub stars** and a rapidly growing ecosystem. It runs entirely in your terminal with a polished TUI (text user interface) and deep LSP integration.

### What You Get for Free

- **Free and open source** — no license fees, no usage caps on the tool itself (LLM API costs apply separately)
- **Terminal-native TUI** with syntax highlighting, file navigation, and inline diffs
- **LSP integration** — real-time diagnostics and code intelligence
- **Multi-session parallel agents** — run multiple AI tasks simultaneously
- **Supports 75+ LLM providers** — OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, local models via Ollama, and more

### The Real Cost

OpenCode is free. The LLM behind it is not (unless you run local models). Typical API costs:

| Provider | Estimated Monthly Cost |
| --- | --- |
| DeepSeek API | $2-5 (light use) |
| Claude Sonnet | $10-20 (moderate use) |
| Claude Opus | $20-50 (heavy use) |
| Local model (Ollama) | $0 (hardware only) |

### Limitations

No visual IDE. No graphical diffs. No autocomplete in the traditional sense. You need to be comfortable in a terminal. Setting up LLM API keys requires some initial configuration.

### Verdict

The best free AI coding tool for developers who live in the terminal. Pair it with a cheap API like DeepSeek for a monthly cost under $5, or run local models for truly $0 usage.

* * *

## 4\. Aider (Open Source)

**Best for:** Developers with git-heavy workflows who want every AI edit tracked as a commit.

Aider is an open-source AI pair programming tool with **39,000+ GitHub stars** and a unique philosophy: every AI-generated edit is automatically committed to git with a descriptive message. This makes AI changes reviewable, revertible, and auditable.

### What You Get for Free

- **Free and open source** (LLM API costs apply separately)
- **Deep git integration** — every AI edit is a git commit
- **Supports 100+ programming languages**
- **Full codebase mapping** — Aider builds a map of your entire repository for context
- **Works with any LLM** — connect your own API key

### Limitations

Like OpenCode, you pay for LLM API calls. Aider is terminal-only. The automatic git commit behavior is either its best feature or its most annoying one, depending on your workflow. No parallel agents.

### Verdict

Ideal if you work in a git-centric workflow and want a clear audit trail of what the AI changed and why. The automatic commit history makes it easy to review or roll back any AI suggestion.

* * *

## 5\. Continue (Open Source)

**Best for:** IDE users who want an open-source alternative to Copilot or Cursor without switching editors.

Continue is the most Copilot-like open-source option, with **20,000+ GitHub stars**. It runs as an extension inside VS Code or JetBrains — no new IDE to learn.

### What You Get for Free

- **Free and open source**
- **Code completion** — inline suggestions like Copilot
- **Chat panel** — ask questions about your code
- **Edit from natural language** — highlight code, describe changes, get diffs
- **Any LLM backend** — OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Ollama, or self-hosted models

### Limitations

Autocomplete latency depends heavily on your LLM provider. Local models are slower than cloud APIs. The extension is less polished than Copilot or Cursor — expect occasional rough edges in diff rendering and multi-file workflows.

### Verdict

The closest free alternative to GitHub Copilot. If you want AI coding inside VS Code without paying for Copilot or Cursor, Continue is the answer. Connect it to a cheap API and you have a capable setup for under $5/month.

* * *

## 6\. Gemini Code Assist (Google)

**Best for:** Developers already in the Google Cloud and Firebase ecosystem.

Google's entry in the AI coding assistant space. Gemini Code Assist is powered by Gemini models and integrates with Google's cloud tooling.

### What You Get for Free

- **Free tier available** — code completions and chat
- **Works in VS Code, JetBrains, and Cloud Shell**
- **Powered by Gemini models** — decent for standard coding tasks
- **Tight Google Cloud integration** — helpful for Firebase, GCP, and Cloud Run workflows

### Limitations

Less capable than Copilot or Claude-powered tools on complex multi-file tasks. The free tier's exact limits are less transparent than Copilot's. The tool shines in Google Cloud contexts but feels generic outside that ecosystem.

### Verdict

Worth using if you are already building on Google Cloud. Not worth switching to from Copilot or open-source tools if you are not in the Google ecosystem.

* * *

## 7\. Amazon Q Developer (AWS)

**Best for:** Developers building on AWS who want AI assistance with infrastructure and cloud code.

Amazon Q Developer (formerly CodeWhisperer) is AWS's AI coding assistant. Its strength is deep AWS integration — IAM policies, CloudFormation templates, Lambda functions, and infrastructure-as-code.

### What You Get for Free

- **Free tier** — code completions across multiple languages
- **Security scans** — automated vulnerability detection in your code
- **AWS service integration** — context-aware suggestions for AWS APIs
- **Works in VS Code and JetBrains**

### Limitations

Heavily AWS-centric. If you are not writing AWS infrastructure code, the suggestions are noticeably less useful than Copilot or Cursor. General-purpose coding assistance is weaker. The AI struggles with frontend and UI tasks.

### Verdict

A no-brainer add-on if you write AWS infrastructure code daily. Not a primary coding assistant for general software development.

* * *

## The Real Cost of "Free"

Every tool on this list has a catch. Here is an honest breakdown:

### Proprietary Free Tiers (Copilot, Cursor, Gemini, Amazon Q)

You get a **limited number of monthly requests**. This works for:

- Weekend project developers
- Students and learners
- Developers evaluating tools before buying

It does not work for full-time professional development. You will hit limits within 1-2 weeks of serious use.

### Open-Source Tools (OpenCode, Aider, Continue)

The tool is genuinely free. The LLM is not. Your real cost depends on which AI model you connect:

| Setup | Monthly Cost | Quality |
| --- | --- | --- |
| OpenCode + Ollama (local CodeLlama) | $0 | Decent for simple tasks, struggles with complex code |
| Continue + DeepSeek API | $2-5 | Good for most tasks, occasional errors |
| Aider + Claude Sonnet API | $10-20 | High quality, handles complex refactoring |
| OpenCode + Claude Opus API | $20-50 | Top-tier quality, comparable to Cursor Pro |

The irony: an open-source tool connected to a premium API can cost more than a Cursor Pro subscription. The advantage is flexibility — you choose your price-quality trade-off and are never locked into a vendor.

* * *

## Best Combinations for Zero-Budget Developers

If your goal is spending as close to $0 as possible, here are practical setups:

### The $0 Setup

- **Continue** in VS Code + **Ollama** running DeepSeek-Coder locally
- Requirements: machine with 16GB+ RAM, decent GPU helps
- Quality: handles autocomplete, simple refactors, and code explanations well
- Limitation: slow on older hardware, struggles with complex multi-file changes

### The $5/Month Setup

- **OpenCode** in terminal + **DeepSeek API** for heavy tasks
- **GitHub Copilot Free** for inline completions in VS Code
- Use Copilot for quick completions, switch to OpenCode for bigger changes
- This combination covers most individual developer needs

### The $10/Month Setup

- **Aider** \+ **Claude Sonnet API** for serious refactoring and codebase-wide changes
- **Continue** in VS Code + DeepSeek for daily completions
- Near-professional quality at half the cost of a Cursor Pro subscription

* * *

## When to Upgrade to Paid

Free tools work. But there are clear signs you have outgrown them:

1. **You hit Copilot's 2,000 completion limit before day 10** — you need unlimited completions
2. **You are spending more on API calls than a subscription costs** — Cursor Pro at $20/month becomes cheaper than $30+ in API bills
3. **You need agent mode** — autonomous multi-file workflows are a paid feature in Cursor and not available in Copilot Free
4. **Your team needs shared context** — enterprise features like team-wide codebase indexing require paid plans
5. **You value autocomplete speed over cost** — Cursor's Supermaven autocomplete and Copilot's native integration are faster than any open-source setup

The transition point for most developers is around **$15-20/month in LLM API spending**. At that point, a paid tool with unlimited usage, faster autocomplete, and polished UX is the better deal.

* * *

## The Bottom Line

The free AI coding landscape in 2026 splits cleanly into two camps:

**Proprietary free tiers** (Copilot, Cursor, Gemini, Amazon Q) give you a limited taste of polished products. Good for getting started, not enough for daily professional use.

**Open-source tools** (OpenCode, Aider, Continue) give you unlimited, flexible AI coding at the cost of setup time and LLM API bills. Good for developers who want control and do not mind the terminal or some rough edges.

The best approach for most developers: start with **GitHub Copilot Free** to learn AI-assisted coding. When you hit limits, try **Continue** or **OpenCode** with a cheap API. If you eventually spend more time fighting free-tier limits than writing code, that is when a paid subscription pays for itself.

## The tools have never been more capable. The barrier to entry has never been lower. The only wrong move is not trying any of them.

### Act mode (execution with approval)

- Creates new files and directories

- Iterates until the task is complete or it needs your input

## Step 8: Auto-Approve, YOLO Mode, and Safety

Approving every action gets old fast. Cline's auto-approve settings let you pre-authorise specific categories of action.

### Auto-approve categories

- **Terminal commands** — auto-approve safe operations or all of them

- **Browser actions** — auto-approve `browser_action` steps

- **MCP tools** — auto-approve specific MCP server calls

The agent classifies each terminal command with a `requires_approval` flag. Build commands, read-only queries, and similar operations are flagged as safe; destructive operations (`rm -rf`, `DROP TABLE`, `force push`) always require explicit approval regardless of auto-approve settings.

A common practical setup for solo work: auto-approve file reads and a small allowlist of safe commands (`npm test`, `npm run lint`, `pnpm build`), require explicit approval for file writes and dependency installs. This keeps you in the loop without grinding the agent to a halt.

### YOLO Mode

YOLO Mode disables every safety check. The Cline docs explicitly warn: **"This is dangerous."** Enabling YOLO Mode auto-approves all actions — file deletion, system modification, network requests, anything. Restrict it to isolated environments (a sandboxed VM, a throwaway branch, a container) and assume nothing about the resulting state.

Cline can post OS-level notifications when approvals are needed or when an auto-approved long-running command crosses 30 seconds. Useful when you're context-switching to email or Slack between iterations.

## Step 9: Checkpoints and Rollback

Cline maintains a **shadow Git repository** — separate from your project's actual Git history — and commits the file state after each tool use. Checkpoints offer three restore modes:

- **Restore Files** — revert files to the snapshot, keep the conversation

- **Restore Task Only** — delete messages after the checkpoint, leave files alone

- **Restore Files & Task** — full reset to the chosen point

Checkpoints capture untracked files too, which is the difference between "I lost a file" and "I lost nothing." Combined with a feature branch and `git stash`, the cost of an experiment that goes sideways drops to roughly zero. This is separate from your real Git history; nothing pollutes your commits unless you commit it yourself.

## Step 10: Best Practices

### Always start with Plan mode

The single most common mistake is jumping straight into Act. Plan mode reads, doesn't write — it costs a fraction of the tokens and catches misunderstandings early. A 30-second planning conversation routinely saves a 10-minute wrong-direction implementation.

### Review every diff

Cline shows you a diff for each file edit. Read it. AI-generated code can contain subtle issues — wrong error handling, missing edge cases, hardcoded values that should be configurable. Pay special attention to:

- **Imports** — right paths, no surprise dependencies?

- **Error handling** — catching the right exceptions, helpful error messages?

- **Naming** — does it match your project's conventions?

- **Side effects** — did it touch files outside the scope you expected?

### Provide rich context with `@` mentions

Cline supports an `@` mention system in chat input:

- `@file` — include a specific file's content

- `@folder` — include a directory tree

- `@url` — fetch and include a URL's content

- `@problems` — include the IDE's current diagnostics

- `@terminal` — include recent terminal output

- `@git` — include current diff or commit history

Specific is cheaper. Instead of "fix the auth", try:

Copy

```
@src/middleware/auth.ts @src/routes/api.ts @AGENTS.md
Add JWT refresh-token rotation to the auth middleware and update the API
routes to handle the new token format. Access tokens expire in 15 minutes,
refresh tokens in 7 days.
```

### Manage costs deliberately

- Start in Plan mode — it's cheaper than rejected Act-mode generations

- Cheap models for boilerplate (Haiku, GPT-4o mini, qwen2.5-coder local) and frontier models for hard reasoning

- Be specific — vague prompts cause wider codebase exploration and bigger token bills

- Break large tasks into smaller ones — "refactor the entire API layer" is a token bonfire; "extract the user-routes module into its own service" is tractable

- Set a spend limit in **Settings → Spending Limits**

### Use feature branches and frequent checkpoints

Feature branch every significant Cline session — Git is your real safety net. Combined with Cline checkpoints, you have two complementary undo systems: Cline for "step back two prompts", Git for "throw the whole branch out".

### Cline vs Cursor vs Claude Code: when to use what

A reasonable 2026 decision tree:

- **Cursor** — AI-first fork of VS Code, best for inline completion and chat-driven micro-edits inside a custom editor

- **Cline** — extension that adds agentic AI to _standard_ VS Code (and JetBrains, Zed, Neovim), best for multi-file autonomous tasks, terminal automation, browser-driven verification

- **Claude Code** — Anthropic's own terminal-native agent, best for headless / CLI workflows, deep MCP integration, agent-to-agent setups

Many teams run two: a tab-completion tool for line-level speed (Copilot or Cursor) and Cline for multi-file work where the agent needs to plan, execute, and verify across the project. They're complementary, not competing — the comparison of AI coding CLIs for deployment workflows breaks down the tradeoffs further, and our broader writeup of how AI coding assistants are changing deployments covers the workflow implications.

## Step 11: Pair Cline with DeployHQ for Git-to-Production

Cline writes the code; DeployHQ ships it. The boundary is clean: Cline owns the local edit/test/debug loop, DeployHQ owns what happens after `git push`. If you'd rather not leave the editor at all, you can also drive DeployHQ deployments straight from your AI editor via MCP — the same pattern maps cleanly onto Cline's MCP support.

### A real Cline-to-DeployHQ workflow

**1\. Plan the feature**

Copy

```
I need to add a /health endpoint to our Express API that checks database
connectivity, Redis connection, and returns the app version from package.json.
Return 200 with JSON when all checks pass; 503 with details about which check
failed otherwise. Use @src/config/database.ts and @src/config/redis.ts for
connection references.
```

Cline reads the codebase in Plan mode and proposes:

- Create `src/routes/health.ts` with the health-check logic

- Add ping helpers for the database and Redis connections

- Register the route in `src/app.ts`
- Add `tests/routes/health.test.ts`

**2\. Switch to Act — Cline implements across files**

Copy

```
// src/routes/health.ts
import { Router, Request, Response } from 'express';
import { pool } from '../config/database';
import { redisClient } from '../config/redis';
import { version } from '../../package.json';

const router = Router();

router.get('/health', async (_req: Request, res: Response) => {
  const checks = { database: false, redis: false };

  try {
    await pool.query('SELECT 1');
    checks.database = true;
  } catch { /* db check failed */ }

  try {
    await redisClient.ping();
    checks.redis = true;
  } catch { /* redis check failed */ }

  const healthy = Object.values(checks).every(Boolean);

  res.status(healthy ? 200 : 503).json({
    status: healthy ? 'healthy' : 'degraded',
    version,
    checks,
    timestamp: new Date().toISOString(),
  });
});

export { router as healthRouter };
```

It registers the route and creates the test file, each diff visible for approval.

**3\. Cline runs the tests**

Copy

```
Cline wants to run: npm test -- --grep "health"
[Approve] [Reject]
```

If a test fails, Cline reads the error, proposes a fix, applies it, and runs again. The implement-test-fix loop continues until the suite is green.

**4\. Review changes in the IDE diff view**

Use the IDE's Source Control panel to review every file Cline created or modified — exactly like reviewing a teammate's pull request.

**5\. Commit, push, let DeployHQ deploy**

Copy

```
git checkout -b feature/health-check
git add -A
git commit -m "Add /health endpoint with database and Redis checks"
git push origin feature/health-check
```

If your DeployHQ project is configured with automatic Git deployments, pushing to your deployment branch triggers the pipeline immediately. DeployHQ:

- Pulls the latest code from your repository ( GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, or self-hosted Git)

- Runs your build pipeline (`npm ci && npm run build`, etc.)

- Transfers files to your server via SFTP, SSH, or a cloud target

- Cuts over with zero downtime — the old release keeps serving traffic until the new release is fully staged

- Keeps every deployment versioned so you can roll back instantly when something does go wrong

### Why the separation matters

Cline stays in your editor. DeployHQ stays in your deployment pipeline. Neither tries to do the other's job, and that boundary buys you:

- **Auditability** — Git history shows what Cline changed; DeployHQ logs show what was deployed and when

- **Rollback safety** — DeployHQ can roll back to any previous deployment independently of what Cline did. You're never locked into AI-generated code

- **Team compatibility** — half the team can use Cline, the other half can use whatever they like; the deployment pipeline doesn't care

- **Build pipeline control** — DeployHQ's build commands handle compilation, minification, and dependency installation server-side, separate from whatever the agent did locally

For a deeper look at running AI agents directly inside CI/CD pipelines, see our writeup on agentic workflows in CI/CD and AI agents in CI/CD: from GitHub issue to production deploy.

If you don't have DeployHQ wired up yet:

2. Connect your Git repository (GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, or any Git host)

3. Configure your server connection (SSH, SFTP, or a cloud provider)

4. Set your build commands — for a typical Node.js project:

Copy

```
npm ci
npm run build
```

1. Enable automatic deployments on your main branch

2. Push from VS Code; DeployHQ deploys. No additional steps.

## Step 12: Troubleshooting

### "Connection failed" or "API key invalid"

- Verify the API key is correct and has credits/quota remaining

- For Anthropic: check the key hasn't been rotated at the Anthropic console

- For OpenRouter: confirm credits are loaded

- For Ollama: confirm the daemon is running (`ollama list`)

- For Cline Provider: re-authenticate with `cline auth` (CLI) or sign in again at app.cline.bot

- v3.79+ enterprise users: confirm Azure Blob Storage credentials if you're using it as the storage backend

### Cline is slow or unresponsive

- Large files balloon token usage and response time — use `@file` to scope to specific files instead of letting Cline scan the workspace

- Local models are slower than cloud APIs; switch providers for hard tasks

- Check the IDE's output panel (View → Output → Cline) for error messages

- v3.80 raised the Node.js heap to 8 GB to fix OOM crashes — if you're on an older version, upgrade

### Cline makes incorrect changes

- Always start in Plan mode and verify the approach

- Provide more context: reference specific files, describe existing patterns, mention constraints

- Use `.clinerules/` to enforce coding standards across sessions

- Roll back via Checkpoints and try a more specific prompt

### High token usage

- Break large tasks into smaller, focused requests

- Use Plan mode to estimate scope before acting

- Switch to a cheaper model for routine work

- Use `@file` to limit codebase exploration

- Enable a spend limit in **Settings → Spending Limits** so a runaway session stops itself

### MCP server won't connect

- Verify the MCP server command works when run manually in your terminal

- Check that env vars are set correctly in `cline_mcp_settings.json`
- Confirm the command path is absolute or on the launchd/systemd `$PATH` (not your interactive shell `$PATH`)

- Look at the MCP server logs in Settings → MCP Servers → \[server name\] → Logs

- For SSE servers, confirm the URL is reachable: `curl -sI <url>`

### Terminal commands fail

- Cline uses the IDE's integrated terminal, which inherits your shell environment

- If commands fail, run them manually in the same terminal first to isolate

- Check that `PATH` includes the necessary tools (Node.js, Python, Docker, etc.)

- On Windows, ensure the right shell is active (PowerShell vs Command Prompt vs WSL)

- v3.80 removed foreground terminal mode — every command now runs as a background task, which fixes a class of stuck-process bugs

### Browser automation broken or returns empty pages

- `browser_action` requires Claude Sonnet (3.5+) — the only model with reliable screen-aware tool support. Other providers will run it but with degraded results

- On Linux, ensure Chromium dependencies are installed (`sudo apt-get install -y libnss3 libatk1.0-0 libgbm1` and friends)

- For headless containers, check that Puppeteer can spawn a sandboxed Chromium — disable AppArmor profiles for `chrome` if needed

## Conclusion

Cline in 2026 is materially different from the "Claude Dev" extension that launched in 2024. The core idea — autonomous, agentic AI inside your editor with explicit per-step approval — is the same; the surface around it has expanded considerably. Plan/Act gives you structured control. The 30+ provider list (plus Cline Provider) means you're never locked to a vendor. `.clinerules/` and conditional rules turn coding standards into version-controlled, file-scoped governance. The MCP Marketplace plus stdio/SSE configuration makes it trivial to plug in databases, observability, and internal tools. Computer Use lets the agent verify its own UI work in a real browser. Spend limits, YOLO mode, and Lazy Teammate Mode let you tune the safety/autonomy trade-off to match the work in front of you.

For developers running serious deployment workflows, pairing Cline with DeployHQ's continuous deployment platform is the natural shape: Cline handles the smart-editor side of your day (writing code, fixing errors, debugging across files, automating browser checks), while DeployHQ handles the production side — running build pipelines, executing atomic deployments, and supporting one-click rollback when something does go wrong.

Asumo que preguntas por **alternativas gratuitas o mejores en Windows 11 para programación asistida por IA / CLI coding**, no por “API” meteorológica ni por normas API de lubricantes. Si era otra cosa, dímelo y lo reconduzco.

## Resumen ejecutivo — comité multidisciplinario

Sí: hay opciones **gratis** y también opciones **mejores** en Windows 11, pero “gratis” casi siempre significa una de estas tres cosas: límites de uso, pago indirecto vía tokens, o costo en hardware local. El informe de NxCode de 2026 describe un mercado dividido entre free tiers limitados y herramientas open source sin suscripción [[59]].

- **Para front-end visual complejo**, Cline sigue siendo una de las opciones gratuitas más completas porque puede editar archivos, ejecutar comandos y verificar interfaz en navegador [[69]].  
- Cline es presentado como asistente gratuito de VS Code por Addy Osmani [[66]].  
- Si necesitas **$0 sin tarjeta**, Kilo Code ofrece Kilo Auto Free sin tarjeta [[72]].  
- Esa capa gratuita tiene límites publicados [[76]].  
- Además existe un reporte de tercero que afirma que el free tier antiguo de Kilo terminó en marzo [[71]].  
- Si prefieres **terminal**, OpenCode incluye modelos gratuitos o conexión a proveedores [[79]].  
- En Windows, OpenCode puede instalarse con Chocolatey o Scoop [[77]].  
- Si buscas **contexto amplio sin pagar**, Gemini CLI ofrece capa gratuita de 60 solicitudes/min y 1.000 solicitudes/día [[119]].  
- Si tu prioridad es **privacidad total**, Continue + Ollama permite una alternativa local y gratuita en Windows [[85]].  
- Si quieres **cero configuración**, GitHub Copilot Free entrega 2.000 autocompletados y 50 chats al mes en VS Code [[93]].  
- Si mides “mejor” por benchmark de terminal, Codex CLI aparece con 83,4% en Terminal-Bench 2.1 [[128]].  

Conclusión rápida: **no hay una herramienta gratuita que sea simultáneamente ilimitada, visual, privada y de máxima calidad** [[59]]. Hay que elegir entre límite, token, hardware o control.

## Triangulación del comité

### 1) Perspectiva científico-técnica

El criterio técnico no es “gratis sí/no”, sino **costo por token, contexto, latencia, capacidad agéntica y acceso a navegador**.

Codex CLI obtiene 83,4% en Terminal-Bench 2.1 según la comparativa de MorphLLM [[128]]. Gemini CLI ofrece 1 millón de tokens de contexto según Developers Digest [[122]]. La capa gratuita de Gemini CLI está limitada a 60 solicitudes por minuto y 1.000 solicitudes por día [[119]]. GitHub Copilot Free está limitado a 2.000 autocompletados y 50 chats mensuales [[93]]. OpenCode soporta más de 75 proveedores de LLM según NxCode [[5]]. OpenCode también aparece con 172K estrellas en la comparativa de MorphLLM [[128]].

En local, el trade-off es claro: los modelos locales permiten costo marginal cero, pero suelen perder calidad frente a modelos cloud para tareas complejas [[59]].

### 2) Perspectiva práctica Windows 11

En Windows 11, la fricción real está en **PATH, PowerShell, WSL, instaladores y permisos**.

OpenCode recomienda WSL en Windows [[2]]. También puede instalarse nativamente con Chocolatey [[77]]. La guía de instalación de OpenCode de 2026 menciona Chocolatey, Scoop, npm, Bun, pnpm y Mise [[78]]. Kilo Code requiere que PowerShell esté correctamente añadido al PATH en Windows [[70]]. Hay issues reportados donde Kilo falla cuando PowerShell no está bien configurado [[73]].

Cline se instala desde el Marketplace de VS Code [[102]]. Cline funciona con múltiples proveedores, incluidos OpenRouter, Anthropic, OpenAI, Google Gemini, AWS Bedrock, Azure y otros [[99]]. Cline separa Plan y Act para aprobar acciones [[64]]. Cline puede usar navegador para verificar UI [[69]]. Cline añadió integración con Chrome local en la versión 3.10 [[115]]. Hay un issue reportado donde `browser_action` falla en WSL [[113]]. En Windows, una guía comunitaria muestra conexión vía PowerShell [[111]].

Continue soporta Windows x64 y Windows ARM [[90]]. Continue puede configurarse con Ollama para ejecución local [[85]]. Continue fue adquirido por Cursor, aunque mantiene código abierto disponible [[87]].

GitHub Copilot Free funciona en VS Code [[93]]. También hay Copilot gratuito limitado en Visual Studio [[92]]. Visual Studio Community es gratuito para estudiantes, open-source e individuos [[53]].

OpenAI lanzó la app Codex para Windows el 4 de marzo de 2026 [[124]]. Codex CLI ofrece instaladores para Windows [[127]]. OpenAI envió Codex Computer Use para Windows el 29 de mayo de 2026 [[129]].

### 3) Perspectiva ético-histórica

El patrón histórico es claro: **los free tiers son embudos de adopción**.

Microsoft presenta Copilot como experiencia básica gratuita, con extras de pago [[156]]. En 2026, reportes de prensa indican que Microsoft reduce o replantea la integración de Copilot en Windows 11 [[140]]. Kilo muestra en 2026 una opción gratuita sin tarjeta [[72]]. Un sitio externo afirma que el free tier antiguo de Kilo terminó en marzo [[71]]. Continue sigue siendo open source tras su adquisición por Cursor [[87]]. Continue publica licencia Apache 2.0 [[90]].

Las herramientas open source no cobran por el cliente, pero trasladan el costo a tokens, infraestructura o hardware [[59]]. Los free tiers propietarios suelen limitar uso, modelos o capacidades agénticas [[59]]. La ejecución local con Ollama/Continue reduce la exposición de datos, pero exige hardware suficiente [[85]].

Microsoft también está construyendo una capa de IA local para Windows con Microsoft Foundry on Windows [[145]].

## Análisis por casos

### Caso 1: Quieres una web visual avanzada con animaciones y $0

**Recomendación principal:** Cline con proveedor gratuito/económico.  
Cline puede usar navegador para verificar UI [[69]]. Cline separa Plan y Act para controlar cambios [[64]]. Cline funciona con múltiples proveedores [[99]].

**Alternativa sin tarjeta:** Kilo Code.  
Kilo ofrece Kilo Auto Free sin tarjeta [[72]]. Kilo tiene límites gratuitos publicados [[76]]. Antes de depender de Kilo, verifica si el plan gratuito cambió [[71]].

**Advertencia:** para animaciones complejas, los modelos gratuitos pueden ser menos fiables que Claude/GPT/Gemini premium [[59]].

### Caso 2: Quieres privacidad total y cero costo por token

**Recomendación:** Continue + Ollama.  
Continue soporta Windows x64 y ARM [[90]]. Continue puede usar Ollama para modelos locales [[85]]. La ejecución local reduce dependencia de APIs externas [[85]].

**Advertencia:** los modelos locales suelen perder calidad en tareas complejas [[59]].

### Caso 3: Quieres terminal pura y máxima compatibilidad con APIs

**Recomendación:** OpenCode.  
OpenCode incluye modelos gratuitos o conexión a proveedores [[79]]. OpenCode puede instalarse con Chocolatey o Scoop [[77]]. OpenCode recomienda WSL en Windows [[2]]. OpenCode soporta más de 75 proveedores [[5]].

**Alternativas:** Gemini CLI ofrece capa gratuita con límites [[119]]. Gemini CLI ofrece contexto de 1M tokens [[122]]. Codex CLI lidera Terminal-Bench según MorphLLM [[128]]. Codex CLI tiene instaladores para Windows [[127]].

### Caso 4: Quieres algo oficial, simple y sin configurar agentes

**Recomendación:** GitHub Copilot Free.  
Copilot Free da 2.000 autocompletados y 50 chats al mes [[93]]. Copilot también tiene uso gratuito limitado en Visual Studio [[92]]. Visual Studio Community es gratis para individuos [[53]].

**Advertencia:** si haces desarrollo intensivo, el límite mensual se queda corto [[93]].

### Caso 5: Si “mejor” significa pagar poco o suscripción

**Recomendación:** Windsurf si quieres IDE pulido.  
Windsurf ofrece free tier con 25 créditos/mes [[28]]. Su plan de entrada cuesta alrededor de $20/mes [[27]].

**Alternativa:** Cline con API premium.  
Cline puede usar proveedores premium sin estar atado a una suscripción única [[99]].

## Comparación densa de opciones gratuitas

### Cline
Cline es un agente open-source con Plan/Act, MCP y flujo terminal-first [[62]]. Addy Osmani lo describe como gratuito y de clase alta para VS Code [[66]]. Cline puede crear/editar archivos, ejecutar comandos y usar navegador con permiso [[69]]. Cline funciona con proveedores múltiples, incluyendo OpenRouter, Anthropic, OpenAI, Google Gemini, AWS Bedrock y Azure [[99]]. Cline permite integración con Chrome local [[115]]. Cline puede ser la mejor opción gratuita si ya tienes una clave API económica o gratuita [[66]].

### Kilo Code
Kilo Code se presenta como agente open source para IDE, CLI y nube [[7]]. Kilo afirma acceso a más de 500 modelos [[8]]. Kilo Auto Free se anuncia sin tarjeta [[72]]. Kilo publica límites para su capa gratuita [[76]]. Un sitio externo dice que el free tier antiguo terminó en marzo [[71]]. En Windows, Kilo requiere PowerShell correctamente configurado [[70]]. Hay issues de Kilo cuando PowerShell no está en PATH [[73]].

### OpenCode
OpenCode es un agente de código abierto para terminal, escritorio o extensión [[2]]. OpenCode ofrece modelos gratuitos incluidos o conexión a proveedores [[1]]. OpenCode puede instalarse en Windows con Chocolatey [[77]]. También puede instalarse con Scoop [[77]]. La guía 2026 menciona npm y otros gestores [[78]]. OpenCode soporta más de 75 proveedores [[5]]. OpenCode es recomendado si quieres una CLI agnóstica y sin suscripción fija [[79]].

### Continue
Continue es una extensión open-source de VS Code con agente, chat, edición y autocompletado [[90]]. Continue soporta Windows x64 y ARM [[90]]. Continue usa licencia Apache 2.0 [[90]]. Continue puede conectarse a Ollama para modelos locales [[85]]. Continue fue adquirido por Cursor [[87]]. Continue mantiene base de código open-source disponible [[87]].

### GitHub Copilot Free
GitHub Copilot Free ofrece 2.000 autocompletados/mes [[93]]. También ofrece 50 solicitudes de chat/mes [[93]]. Copilot Free funciona en VS Code [[93]]. Copilot también tiene versión gratuita limitada en Visual Studio [[92]]. Visual Studio Community es una opción gratuita de IDE para individuos [[53]].

### Gemini CLI
Gemini CLI es un agente open-source de Google para terminal [[120]]. Gemini CLI ofrece free tier de 60 solicitudes/min y 1.000 solicitudes/día [[119]]. Gemini CLI ofrece contexto de 1M tokens según análisis de terceros [[122]]. Gemini CLI es útil para proyectos grandes por contexto [[122]].

### Codex CLI / Codex App
Codex CLI es un agente de OpenAI que corre localmente en terminal [[127]]. Codex CLI ofrece instaladores para Windows [[127]]. La app Codex llegó a Windows el 4 de marzo de 2026 [[124]]. Codex Computer Use llegó a Windows el 29 de mayo de 2026 [[129]]. Codex CLI aparece con 83,4% en Terminal-Bench 2.1 según MorphLLM [[128]].

### Windsurf
Windsurf tiene free tier con 25 créditos/mes [[28]]. Windsurf es considerado un editor AI pulido, con precio de entrada alrededor de $20/mes [[27]]. Si tu prioridad es experiencia visual sin configurar proveedores, Windsurf puede ser mejor que una opción gratuita limitada [[27]].

### Aider
Aider es un agente de programación en terminal [[14]]. Aider es recomendado para desarrolladores senior que trabajan con Git [[19]]. Si tu flujo es Git-heavy, Aider puede ser mejor que Cline para auditoría de cambios [[19]].

### Goose
Goose es un agente open-source de propósito general que corre en tu máquina [[131]]. Goose tiene CLI y aplicación de escritorio [[136]]. Goose aparece en comparativas de herramientas CLI gratuitas [[125]].

## Glosario operativo

**BYOK**: Bring Your Own Key; el usuario aporta su propia clave API. Cline funciona con este enfoque [[64]].

**Agente**: sistema que puede leer, editar, ejecutar y verificar tareas. Cline se describe como agente de codificación [[62]].

**CLI coding**: programación asistida desde terminal. OpenCode es un agente de terminal [[1]].

**Free tier**: capa gratuita con límites. Copilot Free tiene límites mensuales [[93]].

**Token/contexto**: cantidad de información que el modelo puede procesar. Gemini CLI ofrece contexto amplio [[122]].

**Browser action**: capacidad de controlar un navegador para verificar UI. Cline incluye esta capacidad [[69]].

**Plan/Act**: modo de razonamiento y modo de ejecución. Cline usa esta separación [[64]].

**MCP**: Model Context Protocol; estándar para conectar herramientas externas. Cline menciona integración MCP [[62]].

**Ollama**: runtime local para modelos abiertos. Continue puede usar Ollama [[85]].

**WSL**: Windows Subsystem for Linux. OpenCode lo recomienda en Windows [[2]].

**Terminal-Bench**: benchmark de agentes de terminal. Codex CLI aparece bien puntuado allí [[128]].

**Computer Use**: agente que opera interfaz/escritorio. Codex Computer Use llegó a Windows en 2026 [[129]].

## Reflexión prospectiva

El patrón de 2026 es claro: los agentes dejan de ser chatbots y se convierten en procesos que editan, ejecutan, navegan y verifican. OpenAI llevó Codex Computer Use a Windows el 29 de mayo de 2026 [[129]]. Microsoft impulsa IA local con Foundry on Windows [[145]]. Los free tiers seguirán siendo embudos con límites [[59]]. La competencia se desplazará hacia hardware local, privacidad, contexto largo y costo por tarea.
